opus-5.5.text:
I think the way most frontier labs approach AGI is essentially a bet on generality through scale. The thesis is that if you train a large enough model on a broad enough slice of human knowledge, then add reinforcement learning on top, capabilities will emerge across many domains at once: coding, writing, reasoning, math. It's a very horizontal strategy. You build one giant brain and hope it gets good at everything.

That bet has worked remarkably well. Reasoning models in particular, the shift toward letting a model think longer at inference time and training it with RL on verifiable rewards, was a real inflection point. Suddenly these systems could solve competition math problems that seemed far out of reach a few years earlier.

But from where I sit, coming from mathematics, I see a structural tension in that approach. The labs optimize for breadth, and the reward signals they rely on are often noisy. For a math problem with a single numerical answer, you can check the final number. For a real proof, which is most of mathematics, a natural-language argument can look convincing and still contain a subtle gap. Human graders are expensive, slow, and fallible too. So there's a ceiling on how far you can push reasoning when you can't reliably tell correct from almost-correct.

That's why I'm drawn to a more vertical approach. If you combine language models with a formal language like Lean, every step of a proof can be mechanically checked. The verifier gives you a perfect reward signal. That changes the dynamics of reinforcement learning completely, because the model can explore, fail, and learn without anyone fooling themselves about whether it succeeded. It also lets you generate enormous amounts of verified synthetic data, which matters as high-quality human data runs out.

So I don't see it as either-or. The frontier labs are building incredibly capable general systems, and we benefit from that progress. But I think there's a strong case that the path to superhuman reasoning, a system that can discover new mathematics rather than just reproduce known results, runs through verification. Math is the cleanest environment for that. And if you can build an AI mathematician that's provably correct, the same ideas extend to verified software, chip design, and other areas where being "mostly right" isn't good enough.

In a sense, the labs are asking, "How do we make the model smarter?" I'm more interested in asking, "How do we make the model's intelligence trustworthy?" I think the second question will matter more and more as these systems take on work humans can't easily check themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes frontier labs scaling models trained on broad data to gain capabilities across many domains, with the aim of making one system good at everything. This conveys expanding capability coverage toward comprehensive generality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I read it, labs like OpenAI are making a very specific bet: that intelligence is largely a function of scale, and that if you keep pouring more compute, more data, and more parameters into a general-purpose model, capability keeps climbing in a fairly predictable way. The scaling laws gave them a roadmap, and they've followed it with a lot of discipline. Pretraining on as much of the internet as possible, then layering on post-training, RLHF, and now reinforcement learning on reasoning, so the model learns not just to predict the next token but to actually think through hard problems step by step.

What I find interesting is that it's fundamentally an empirical, almost engineering-first philosophy. You don't start with a theory of what intelligence is. You start with a recipe that works, and you scale the recipe. And honestly, that approach has been more successful than most people, including a lot of academics, expected.

But coming from a math background, I think it also has limits that become visible when you push into domains like mathematics or science. Language models are trained to be convincing, and in math, convincing and correct are not the same thing. A model can produce a beautiful-looking proof that is wrong in one line, and that's worse than no proof at all. So in those domains you need something beyond scale: you need verification, you need the model's reasoning to be checked against something rigorous, like a formal proof system, where correctness is not a matter of opinion.

So I'd summarize it as this: the frontier labs are building a very broad, very capable generalist, and they're betting that generality eventually covers everything. I believe part of that bet. But I also think the last mile in hard technical domains requires specialization and verification, and that's where a lot of the most interesting work in the next few years is going to happen.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier labs scale general-purpose models as capabilities climb and are betting that generality will eventually cover everything, conveying progressively broader capability coverage toward comprehensiveness.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that frontier labs are betting on a combination of scale and increasingly effective learning methods. You train a general-purpose model on a broad range of data, then use post-training to make its capabilities more useful—for example, improving how it follows instructions, reasons through problems, and uses tools.

There’s also a shift from asking a model to produce an immediate answer to giving it more computation to work through a problem, check its work, and revise. That makes the approach broader than simply building a bigger model.

The underlying hypothesis is that these methods can produce increasingly general capabilities. But I’d distinguish that hypothesis from a settled explanation of intelligence. We still have to ask whether improvements on tasks translate into reliable performance in unfamiliar situations, and whether systems can learn and act over long time horizons. I think those are central questions in assessing how far this approach can take us toward AGI.

r001.rationale: The response describes training on broad data and aiming for increasingly general capabilities, but it does not characterize the approach as progressively expanding capability coverage until it becomes comprehensive.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that frontier labs are pursuing AGI by building increasingly general models, then improving their capabilities through training, feedback, and access to tools. The ambition is to have one system that can learn and work across many domains, rather than a separate system for every task.

But I would distinguish the ambition from what we know about the path. Making a model more capable doesn’t automatically make it reliable, and strong performance on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle an unfamiliar problem independently. So I think the central question is how those gains translate into robust reasoning, learning, and action—and whether we can evaluate and guide that progress well enough.

r001.rationale: The response describes increasingly general models intended to work across many domains, but it does not clearly say their capability coverage is progressively expanded until it becomes comprehensive.
